tropes.html: Bryan puts a twist on this technique by using a pistol to choke an elderly Albanian against a wall

tropes.name: The Coats Are Off
tropes.html: Bryan at the end.

tropes.name: Concealment Equals Cover
tropes.html: Averted when Bryan is shot at through a wall.

tropes.name: Crazy-Prepared
tropes.html: It comes as part of Bryan's job as a bodyguard to always have the necessary equipment needed to make sure that he can get out of any situation, but this film is where it's really shown. For the trip to Istanbul, he brings himself a suitcase full of recording equipment, cash and passports accessible at a moment's notice, plus a hidden cell phone and even a couple hand grenades just in case. These preparations prove handy when Kim tells him that strange men have entered the hotel she's in.

tropes.name: Cycle of Revenge
tropes.html: Discussed in the final confrontation between Bryan and Murad. Murad tells Bryan that if he kills him, then his other two sons will seek revenge too, to which Bryan ensures him that they'll die the same way. Bryan mentions, however, that Murad can instead go home and spend time with his sons and grandchildren; his killing of Marko is merely the price of being in a criminal business like human trafficking, and echoes the loss of all the lives Marko ruined.

tropes.name: Delayed Reaction
tropes.html: At the living room where several Albanians are watching soccer on TV, the Albanian who decides to exit takes a while to properly react to Bryan suddenly appearing with a gun at his face, only walking back while dropping his things, then screaming just before Bryan shoots him dead and the other Albanians realize they're in danger right at that moment.

tropes.name: Disney Villain Death
tropes.html: In the climax, Bryan takes advantage of the multi-floor balconies around him by dropping Mooks from them, whether it be by shooting them down or throwing them off.

tropes.name: The Don
tropes.html: Murad.

tropes.name: Dramatic Gun Cock
tropes.html: Bryan's cue to duck before two mooks unleash a hail of assault rifle fire through the wall at him.

tropes.name: Drives Like Crazy
tropes.html: Subverted while playing it straight. Kim has failed her driver's license test twice now, yet she can drive perfectly when Bryan is giving her instructions. Guess who has to drive wildly through the streets of Istanbul while avoiding the police, and who's giving them the orders?

tropes.name: Driving Stick
tropes.html: Guess what kind of car is used in the aforementioned chase.

tropes.name: Due to the Dead
tropes.html: After defeating Suko, The Brute of the Albanians, Bryan appears to close his eyes in respect for the toughest fight of his life, though it's not visually clear.

tropes.name: Empathy Doll Shot
tropes.html: In their interrogation on Jean-Claude, one of the Albanians shows him his son's teddy bear to clarify that they're willing to kill not only him but also his family (although it's ambiguous whether they already did the latter or are threatening that they'll do it) if he doesn't give them any information about Bryan's whereabouts.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Loved Ones
tropes.html: Uh oh, Bryan, did we mention that the kidnappers you killed have families and friends in Albania, and they're VERY angry with you now?

tropes.name: Evil Counterpart
tropes.html: Murad comes off as something of an evil Bryan with his Papa Wolf characterization, as well as sporting a similar Badass Longcoat once.

tropes.name: Famous-Named Foreigner
tropes.html:
So, can we conclude that Murad Hoxha is related to the late communist ruler of Albania?
  • Hoxha originally was a Turkish title (Hoca).

tropes.name: Faux Affably Evil
tropes.html: Murad. There's a trope-defining scene where Lenore is talking to him, and Murad mentions how he admires her, how he thinks she's a innocent woman who had nothing to do with his son's death, and then he says for such respect he'll send her back home... in pieces.

tropes.name: Flashback
tropes.html: There are plenty of them made by reusing footage from the first movie. Later, there's also a few from earlier scenes in the film itself.

tropes.name: Foregone Conclusion
tropes.html: At the end, Murad says that he has two sons that will avenge him if he dies at Bryan's hands. Without batting an eye, Bryan says he'll just kill them too if that's the case. And sure enough, they're not in the third movie, although whether it was because of that or something else is unknown.

tropes.name: Fruit Cart
tropes.html: A few of them get smashed during the sequence where Bryan tries to get away from the Albanians going after him on car. Not just fruit carts either; bagels and a few other carts.

tropes.name: Genre Blindness
tropes.html: Despite having a pretty good idea of what Bryan is capable of, Murad still insists on prolonging his suffering and explaining what he intends to do to Bryan's family, then proceeds to not have a few dozen mooks with guns trained on him at all times. This turns out to be exactly as bad a plan as it sounds.

tropes.name: Gilligan Cut
tropes.html: The scene with the background check joke segues directly into Bryan arriving at the house of Kim's boyfriend Jamie.

tropes.name: Googling the New Acquaintance
tropes.html: When Bryan finds out that Kim has a new boyfriend named Jamie, the first thing he does is run a background check on the latter... just as he did with all her other previous boyfriends. Lenore tells him to not run a background check on Jamie, because she knows that he ALWAYS does this.

tropes.name: Groin Attack
tropes.html: Suko stabs Jean-Claude's genitals with scissors to torture him.

tropes.name: Hot Pursuit
tropes.html: Lampshaded. Bryan had to shoot a cop just to ensure that Kim and himself could even get away from the bad guys' hideout, and he flat-out says it. On top of that, the cab they were driving was stolen.

tropes.name: Hypocrite
tropes.html: The Albanians want revenge on Bryan for killing their relatives and friends, and are totally unwilling to accept said relatives' own responsibility for the countless families they ruined in conducting their sex slavery operation, not to mention the fact that Bryan's actions were motivated by the exact same behavior the Albanians condemn him for.

tropes.name: I Did What I Had to Do
tropes.html: Both Bryan and Kim end up committing numerous criminal offenses throughout Istanbul just to get Lenore back.Examples includeDitching a taxi cab without paying the cabbie, then stealing it; throwing hand grenades in a populated area (albeit at targets that are definitely unoccupied); shooting a police officer and evading the police; and, lastly, numerous counts of property damage. They were in the heat of the moment, so they didn't have much time to think about what they're doing. Nearly all of this would typically be handled by the US Embassy and they'd get off without much hassle, but Bryan has to call his buddy Sam to pull some strings at the embassy just to make sure the US military doesn't shoot them as they barrel their way inside.note The ground that embassies are built on is officially deemed part of its country. Any crimes committed by a US citizen in a US Embassy would be prosecuted as if they were committed stateside. Nearly killing US soldiers on US soil definitely counts.

tropes.name: I Have Your Wife
tropes.html: Technically, she's his ex-wife, but the trope still applies.

tropes.name: Impaled with Extreme Prejudice
tropes.html: Murad ends up hanging by a towel hook impaled in his brain stem.

tropes.name: Ironic Echo
tropes.html:
Murad's funeral speech in the Villain Opening Scene parallels Bryan's quote-worthy threat from the first movie, especially the "I will find you" part.
Murad: He slaughtered our men, our brothers, our sons. The dead cry out to us... for justice. On their souls, I swear to you. The man who took our loved ones from us, the man who has brought us such pain and sorrow. We will find him. We will bring him here. We will not rest until his blood flows into this very ground. We will have our revenge.

tropes.name: It's All About Me
tropes.html: As Bryan accuses to Murad, the Albanians' motivation for avenging their relatives is not out of a sense of justice (which is what Murad proclaims), but simply because their losses hurt them. For Murad's case, see Moral Myopia below.

tropes.name: It Works Better with Bullets
tropes.html:
• In one of the trope's finest-ever uses, the abductors shoot a random hotel guest.
  • Bryan pulls this trick on Murad.

tropes.name: Last-Second Chance
tropes.html: Bryan tries to offer Murad a chance to walk away in exchange for leaving them in peace. Murad blows it by going for Bryan's discarded gun.

tropes.name: Maybe Ever After
tropes.html: It's implied at the end that Bryan and Lenore will reunite as a couple, but they don't officially do so on screen.

tropes.name: Mexican Standoff
tropes.html: The brief fight with several Albanians that leads up to Bryan and Lenore's kidnapping ends up in this situation for a moment, until another Albanian squad comes in to solve the conflict in the Albanians' favor.

tropes.name: Mirror Character
tropes.html: Two Papa Wolves square off over their children, both of them willing to break laws and endanger others if it gets them what they want.

tropes.name: Moe Greene Special
tropes.html: Bryan performs this on one of the Mooks in the climax with one of the many bullet holes said mook and his partner (who calls him "Mirko") left following a barrage of shots through a wall.

tropes.name: Moral Myopia
tropes.html: Invoked by Murad. Bryan killed his son, and that makes him the bad guy. The fact that Marko was practically a mass murderer to begin with, having condemned an unknown number of girls to a short life of sexual slavery, is irrelevant to the calculations. Murad even cheerfully tells Bryan that he intends to finish Marko's job of selling Kim as a sex slave.

tropes.name: Neck Snap
tropes.html: With many enemies, it looks like they are dying from a simple touch administered by Bryan, thanks to the removal of the crisp "crunching" sound to secure a PG-13 rating.

tropes.name: Newspaper-Thin Disguise
tropes.html: Done by one of the Albanians while he watches after Bryan.

tropes.name: Non-Action Big Bad
tropes.html: Much like his son in the first movie, pistols are the only means of fighting that Murad uses. Plus, arguing with Bryan is all he directly does against him, and he attempts to fight in the wrong time and situation for him.

tropes.name: Not a Game
tropes.html: Not a Game

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html: Bryan makes a deal with Murad to end this war between him and Murad's family. Murad goes back on it and immediately comes to the realization that it was a very bad idea.

tropes.name: The Patriarch
tropes.html: Murad.

tropes.name: Photographic Memory
tropes.html: Bryan takes this trope to truly frightening levels. He was able to trace his steps back to where he and Lenore were held by the kidnappers in spite of being blind-folded on their first ten minute long trip, by remembering the sounds he heard on the way and how far/long the spaces are between each sound. Eek.

tropes.name: Railroad Tracks of Doom
tropes.html: In the car chase scene, the second of two Albanian drivers going after the taxi Kim and Bryan are on is tricked into passing through a railroad track just in time to get crushed by an incoming train.

tropes.name: Red Shirt
tropes.html: The security officers at the hotel.

tropes.name: Revenge Before Reason
tropes.html: Murad was really Bullying a Dragon. Had he quietly restarted the trafficking ring and kept under Bryan's radar rather than seeking vengeance, he might have avoided all this.

tropes.name: Revenge by Proxy
tropes.html: Bryan killed their families? The Albanians will kill his ex-wife and sell his daughter like the last time.

tropes.name: Revenge Myopia
tropes.html:
Murad explicitly says he doesn't care what his son did to invite Bryan's wrath, only that Bryan killed him. Worse yet, he intends to finish what his son started and outright tells this to Bryan, knowing it will more than likely press the latter's Berserk Button.
Bryan: I killed your son because he kidnapped my daughter!
Murad: [slaps Bryan] I DON'T CARE WHAT HE DID! I only know... I will never see his face again, I will never hear his voice. (kisses Marko's photo) And as you held him responsible for your daughter, I hold you responsible for him!

tropes.name: Revised Ending
tropes.html: The film originally had a different ending than the one that ended up in cinemas. In the original ending, Bryan rescues Lenore from Murad's men before going to the Embassy and she is the one who gives Kim directions while Bryan shoots the cars chasing them. They crash into the Embassy, call Sam for help and cuddle as a family while they wait for the all clear. A representative comes to greet them and Bryan introduces Kim and Lenore with an awkward moment because he doesn't know how to describe his and Lenore's relationship. He decides to go after Murad and Lenore follows him, asking what he's going to do. Bryan replies, "What I do best," and turns to go. Lenore watches him leave before turning to comfort Kim. Bryan tracking and fighting Murad and his men is the same as the theatrical version only without Lenore's scenes. After this, the ending continues as it did in the theatrical cut with Kim passing her driving test and them going out for milkshakes with a surprise appearance by Jamie. Olivier Megaton felt that Bryan going after Murad and his men after Lenore and Kim were safe put his actions into a morally grey area that he was uncomfortable with, so he prolonged Lenore's rescue to make Bryan's actions more justifiable.

tropes.name: Right on the Tick
tropes.html: Bryan is giving his daughter a driving lesson at 2 PM and waits in the car until the exact second the clock strikes 2. Averted later on, when he deliberately waits an extra minute.

tropes.name: Roofhopping
tropes.html: Done by Kim and two Albanians coming after her during a rooftop chase scene. One of said Albanians accidentally hits a hanging wire and falls to the ground in his attempt.

tropes.name: Scenery Porn
tropes.html: The shots of Istanbul and the cemetery in Albania.

tropes.name: Secret Test of Character
tropes.html: Bryan administers one to Murad. He fails.

tropes.name: Sequel Hook
tropes.html:
In spite of Luc Besson claiming that there will be no more Taken movies at the time of Taken 2's release, someone else in the production (likely Olivier Megaton or the executives) HAD to leave an opening for a third movie:
Bryan: You have other sons?
Murad: Two.
  • To be fair about that exchange, though, Bryan immediately points out that he'll kill those two sons too. Whether said third movie would have had the involvement of Besson was another story altogether. Ironically, this hook wasn't followed up on in the actual Taken 3, which ended up having Besson on board once again.

tropes.name: Stuff Blowing Up
tropes.html: Much more so than in the first movie.

tropes.name: Shell-Shocked Veteran
tropes.html: Kim clearly isn't over getting kidnapped in the first movie, and she has a flashback the instant she hears Bryan telling her that he and her mother are going to be taken.

tropes.name: Tap on the Head
tropes.html: Subverted. The final fight is not filled with flashy moves and both sides end up getting really hurt. Suko actually dies because Bryan throws him down and makes him hit his head on a concrete corner.

tropes.name: Took a Level in Badass
tropes.html: Kim reacts rather rationally to the kidnapping of her mother, roofhops in Istanbul, faces an Albanian at gunpoint, performs combat driving that would make Jason Statham wince; and most importantly of all, gaining the courage to rescue her parents alone rather than running to the safety of the American Embassy and letting them die, in spite of not possessing any combat training herself. Only time will tell if she will live up to her father's legacy as a warrior.

tropes.name: Third Time's The Charm
tropes.html: Kim passes her driving test on the third try.

tropes.name: Too Happy to Live
tropes.html: Bryan's family.

tropes.name: Took a Level in Jerkass
tropes.html: Stuart, who helped secure a private flight for Bryan in the first film, abruptly cancels the family spring break trip.

tropes.name: Uncertain Doom
tropes.html:
• Jean-Claude vanishes from the series after this film's scene where the Albanians torture him for information on Bryan's whereabouts. One can only assume that they killed him once they got what they wanted...
  • It's also unclear what happened to Jean-Claude's wife and children.

tropes.name: Unwilling Suspension
tropes.html: In the sequel, Lenore gets put in a painful-looking suspended hogtie by the Albanians. Definitely not the usual Fanservice example for a woman, as she's fully clothed, hooded, and bleeding to death.

tropes.name: Villains Out Shopping
tropes.html: In one of the rooms where the Albanians operate at, several members are initially seen watching a soccer match on television while eating and drinking. They prefer to keep doing that when Murad notifies them that he's going outside due to the trackers being unable to find Kim. Bryan later shows up just in time to interrupt their fun with a fight.

tropes.name: Villains Want Mercy
tropes.html: Murad after failing Bryan's Secret Test of Character, subtly enough. His feared expression had "plead for mercy" written all over it. Bryan doesn't give the bastard time to beg for his life and kills him.

tropes.name: Watching the Sunset
tropes.html: Watching the Sunset

tropes.name: What Measure Is a Mook?
tropes.html: While Bryan kills or knocks out most of the Albanian Mooks without mercy, he offers Murad a second chance in their post-climactic confrontation.

tropes.name: You Killed My Father
tropes.html: The villains are motivated by taking revenge on Bryan for killing their relatives (as well as their friends) in the first film. A specific example, aside from Murad's son Marko, is Suko mentioning to Jean-Claude that Bryan killed his brother and an unspecified number of friends.

tropes.name: Artifact Title
tropes.html:
According to Liam Neeson, nobody gets taken this time. Although depending on how you interpret the story, Lenore is "taken" from Bryan when she is murdered.
  • Stuart does kidnap Kim in the climax and Bryan has to go rescue her.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Biology
tropes.html:
Once Lenore got her throat sliced, there should have been far more blood on her corpse than there was in the movie, considering that the jugular would've pumped a lot of it out all over her clothes.
  • Except that, as we learn later, Lenore was not killed in his apartment, but killed elsewhere then her body was planted by the Russians. We can assume that when they killed her they positioned her in a manner where the blood wouldn't spill all over her. That and too much blood might have taken away the PG-13 rating.

tropes.name: Big Bad
tropes.html: At first, it seems to be Russian mafia boss Oleg Malankov, but it's later revealed that Stuart's been pulling the strings and had Lenore killed to collect her life insurance to pay off Malankov. That said, Malankov still serves as the villain of the climactic fight.

tropes.name: Bloodless Carnage
tropes.html: Being a PG-13 action flick, several characters get shot without much blood. Even the scene of Lenore's corpse, which involved a Slashed Throat, doesn't have as much blood as there would've been in real life.

tropes.name: Bulletproof Human Shield
tropes.html: Bryan uses a thug he's fighting as a shield against another thug opening fire on him with an assault rifle, with the first thug's body easily stopping an entire magazine's worth.

tropes.name: Clear My Name
tropes.html: Bryan is set up for the murder of Lenore.

tropes.name: Dialogue Reversal
tropes.html: At least in the trailer. Dotzler warns Bryan over the phone that all of law enforcement will be coming after him. His response? "Good luck".

tropes.name: Elephant in the Living Room
tropes.html: In the trailer, Dotzler recaps Bryan's background to his agents, pointing out that he's a trained sniper and explosives expert, and his service record comes to a strange dead end, which itself is quite telling. It would hopefully tip him off to the fact that Bryan wouldn't be stupid enough to kill Lenore using a knife with his fingerprints on it, in their house. If not, then it'd be this trope.

tropes.name: I Know You Know I Know
tropes.html: Dotzler is so highly intelligent that he's able to predict what Bryan is doing at that moment (like he knows that it would be useless to follow the GPS on the cellphone just seconds after Bryan puts it on a bus), and Bryan in turn predicts what the cops are going to do and works it into his plans.

tropes.name: Instant Death Bullet
tropes.html: The victim in the opening scene dies instantly after a shot to the guts.

tropes.name: Ironic Echo
tropes.html:
Bryan's threat gets another one in the form of Stuart's explanation to Bryan about why Malankov's mob is after him.
Bryan: They would have killed her someplace else, so why are they coming after me?
Stuart: Because I told them who you were, that you would find them and kill them.

tropes.name: Letters 2 Numbers
tropes.html: Though neither marketed nor actually titled as such, the film is stylized as Tak3n on its DVD and Blu-ray cover art.

tropes.name: The Lost Lenore
tropes.html: Literally.

tropes.name: Mundane Made Awesome
tropes.html: The infamous frenetic cutting during Bryan's Chain-Link Fence climbing scene.

tropes.name: Not Quite Saved Enough
tropes.html: Despite Bryan dispatching a few dozen Mooks to rescue her in the second movie, Lenore is murdered in the third movie. Downplayed as both events are independent from each other.

tropes.name: Nothing Personal
tropes.html: Malankov tells Bryan that Lenore was just part of a business deal, "like many before her."

tropes.name: Please Kill Me if It Satisfies You
tropes.html:
When he loses the final fight to Bryan, Malankov allows the latter to kill him off, even saying that he deserves to die.
"First, he gets me to kill your wife, then you. And when that doesn't work, he pushes you to kill me, no? Either way, he wins. Your wife was just part of a business deal, like many before her. It is my turn to lose the game. Finish me! Finish me! I deserve it!"

tropes.name: The Reveal
tropes.html: Lenore wasn't killed by any of Bryan's enemies from the previous films; it was all arranged by her husband Stuart St. John in order to get 12 million dollars in insurance money.

tropes.name: Slashed Throat
tropes.html: How Lenore is killed.

tropes.name: Sudden Sequel Death Syndrome
tropes.html: Lenore.

tropes.name: Uncertain Doom
tropes.html: We don't know Sam's fate after the films' events. Last we see him, he's unconscious after having been shot by Stuart, and while a cop says he's still alive when they find him, we never found out if he survived.

tropes.name: Water Torture
tropes.html: The waterboarding variant is how Bryan interrogates Stuart after capturing him.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html: We're not quite sure what becomes of Stuart after he's arrested. Bryan promises him that he'll come for him after he inevitably gets acquitted or a short jail sentence because of his connections, but it's not clear if Stuart would later pull a Better to Die than Be Killed to avoid whatever Bryan has planned for him, if Bryan winds up killing him eventually, or even if he ends up executed (another outcome that's implied here).

tropes.name: Wrongful Accusation Insurance
tropes.html: Bryan commits a massive number of crimes in the course of trying to clear his name and later rescue Kim again. Some probably couldn't be proven, and others the police might not pursue (such as those against Russian gangsters). Others, however, were against them: attacking the officers who tried to arrest him, breaking into the LAPD database, hijacking a police car and kidnapping the officer inside, etc. Yet the only one of these which is even mentioned is the breaking into the database (probably the most minor of them) and he's let off completely on all of them. It's very unlikely the police would let crimes against them slide so easily. Then again, he does help them catch the real murderer and take out part of the local Russian mob for them, so that's probably why Dotzler lets him go.

tropes.name: You Don't Look Like You
tropes.html: Due to his switch in actors who look nothing alike between his two appearances, Stuart looks very different in the third movie from the first one. On top of lacking facial hair, he looks a lot younger.

tropes.name: You Killed My Father
tropes.html: Bryan says this almost word-for-word to Malankov: "You killed my ex-wife."

tropes.name: Call-Forward
tropes.html: In the Pilot, Mike Hall tells Bryan that for the sake of not having to make the same choice Mike did, Bryan should avoid having children, especially a daughter. Considering Kim's existence, it's clear that Bryan is not going to take this to heart.

tropes.name: Good Is Not Soft
tropes.html: Hart's team will go to some pretty extreme lengths to protect the US from any threats, starting with the Jack Bauer Interrogation Technique and going up from there.

tropes.name: His Name Is...
tropes.html: CIA agent Clara Ward is killed right as she is about to tell Hart who killed the Senator.

tropes.name: Prequel
tropes.html: Of sorts. It is a modern day origin story showing how Bryan Mills gained his skills.

tropes.name: Race Lift
tropes.html: Sam Gilroy was played by a white Leland Orser in the film series. In the show, he is played by Michael Irby who is mixed race.

tropes.name: Saved by Canon
tropes.html: Being a prequel exploring Mills' life prior to the Taken films, he is going to survive whatever is thrown at him.

tropes.name: Token Romance
tropes.html: Bryan and Asha. They are quickly thrown together at the start of season 1 and their romance is definitely the B plot to Bryan gaining his 'skills'. Plus, even before the cast shakeup prior to season 2, we know they won't last since this series is a prequel to the film series - therefore we know Bryan still has to meet Lenore so they can have Kim.

tropes.name: Unusual Euphemism
tropes.html: The team refers to the Mooks they encounter as "tourists".

tropes.name: 2D Visuals, 3D Effects
tropes.html: All three builds of Roger's game display this. The gameplay environments are all CG with 2D sprites of the characters. Interestingly enough, the designs for Pongo and two of the puppies (Patches and Whizzer) in the footage are from the original 1961 film, with the dogcatcher and the plumber drawn in a similar style. Cruella's design in the game is based directly on Glenn Close herself rather than the original Marc Davis design from the film, but reverted back to the Marc Davis design in the tie-in game.

tropes.name: Abnormal Limb Rotation Range
tropes.html: The mouse in DeVil Manor makes its tail straight and points it diagonally down and to the left for Kipper, in order to point him in the direction to find the puppies.

tropes.name: Accidental Misnaming
tropes.html: Cruella never gets Roger's name right (This trope is repeated in the TV series.)

tropes.name: Adaptational Attractiveness
tropes.html: Glenn Close's Cruella is certainly more good looking than her animated counterpart. It's unavoidable since Glenn Close is a stunner herself.

tropes.name: Adaptational Badass
tropes.html:
• The police were completely useless in the animated film. Here, they not only arrest Cruella quickly after finding her stash of illegal furs but also rescue the puppies and give them a ride home.
  • Anita gets some key moments. She clonks Roger in the face to rescue Perdita, whom Roger had mistaken for Pongo, and explains she keeps bricks in her purse for that purpose. Later, she is the one who gives the final refusal to Cruella about selling the puppies, though Roger is the first to declare it.
  • And speaking of Roger, he's much firmer and less stuttery when standing up to Cruella.
  • To say nothing for Lucky. During the dognapping, he is the only one to attempt to fight back against the Baduns, biting Jasper on the hand.

tropes.name: Adaptational Intelligence
tropes.html: The Dearlys, Nanny and the police serve as this. When the puppies are kidnapped, Anita is more than open to the possibility that Cruella took them for petty reasons and realizes it when she finds her Dalmatian coat drawing. Nanny intuits that Perdita and Pongo have gone to search for the puppies, and she is right. Meanwhile, the police do find the evidence that Cruella is the most likely suspect to take the puppies and she's arrested for having other illegal furs, including a tiger that was killed for her skin in London Zoo earlier in the film. They also rescue the puppies, Pongo and Perdita, giving them a ride home.

tropes.name: Adaptational Job Change
tropes.html: Instead of working as a songwriter as in the original version, Roger is an American game developer.

tropes.name: Adaptational Name Change
tropes.html: Kipper, the Airedale Terrier who finds the puppies in the film, is named "Griffin" in the Tiger Electronics handheld game based on the film.

tropes.name: Adaptational Nationality
tropes.html: While Roger is an American residing in London, the original book and animated movie depict him as an Englishman given the nationality of the book and its author, Dodie Smith. Considering the part was offered to Hugh Grant, it's likely the change was made simply to accommodate the casting of Jeff Daniels.

tropes.name: Adaptational Villainy
tropes.html:
• The Badun brothers, and in particular, Jasper. In the animated version, Horace and Jasper had no real loyalty towards Cruella, and served her primarily only for money, but also out of fear and intimidation from their boss. In the live-action version, the brothers are not only portrayed as more loyal towards Cruella, but Jasper has fewer qualms about committing animal cruelty. This is best exemplified when Jasper suggests killing the puppies even when someone else (Skinner) was supposed to be doing it for them.
    Jasper: Right.... time to let the little yappers have it.
    Horace: We ain't supposed to do that, that's Skinner's job!
    Jasper: Well, Skinner isn't here, is he? Besides, I don't see why that little runt should have all the fun.
  • In the original film, only Pongo and Perdita's fifteen puppies were stolen whereas the other eighty-four were bought and paid for. In this version, all ninety-nine puppies were stolen, though at the end of the film a policeman tells Roger and Anita that the other eighty-four don't appear to have owners.

tropes.name: Adaptation Name Change
tropes.html: Hell Hall is instead called De Vil Manor.

tropes.name: Adaptation Relationship Overhaul
tropes.html: The original book and the animated adaptation mention that Anita and Cruella were schoolmates and friends as children. In this film, Cruella is Anita's employer and mentor, with a notable age gap between them.

tropes.name: All There in the Manual
tropes.html: Two of the non-Dalmatians in the film, Kipper (an Airedale Terrier) and Fogey (an Old English Sheepdog), don't have their names given in the film itself, but are in the credits and merchandise.

tropes.name: Animal Reaction Shot
tropes.html:
• Pongo and Perdita have more than their fair share of yawns and nods and embarrassed looks.
  • Played for Laughs during the ending, as the puppies all tilt their heads in line with the minecart in the game, and flip their ears up wih and Oh, Crap! expression upon seeing Cruella in the game.

tropes.name: Animal Talk
tropes.html: There's a scene where Pongo and a bird communicate with each other.

tropes.name: Animated Adaptation
tropes.html: Sort of. Cartoon versions of these movies' unique puppies have been featured on tie-in merchandise, and a few characters from the movie made it into the cartoon series.

tropes.name: Arson, Murder, and Jaywalking
tropes.html:
Horace lists the many things wrong with his and Jasper's current assignment.
Horace: I'll be honest with you, mate! This job is fast losing its charm! The housing stinks, the food's lousy, the lavatory facilities are appalling, and so far, we haven't been paid so much as one quid!
Jasper: Oh, will you stop moaning?! Look, this time tomorrow night, it's all over. We get our boodle, we'll be outta here before you can say dead puppies.

tropes.name: Ash Face
tropes.html: Horace, after the Banana in the Tailpipe moment below.

tropes.name: Babies Ever After
tropes.html: Roger and Anita have a little girl at the end, while the puppies grow up with puppies of their own. And it seems like Roger and Anita are about to have another.

tropes.name: Bag of Kidnapping
tropes.html: This is how Jasper and Horace steal the puppies.

tropes.name: Banana in the Tailpipe
tropes.html: Raccoons put a large nut in the tailpipe of the bad guys' truck. The pressure does shoot the nut out eventually - when Horace is examining the tail pipe.

tropes.name: Battle Discretion Shot
tropes.html: Jasper punching Horace for commenting on Mr. Skinner's scar after the former explicitly tells him not to is not shown to the audience as Jasper closes the door before the punch. It would be too violent for a G rating if it was actually shown.

tropes.name: Be Careful What You Wish For
tropes.html:
Horace, freezing cold after dropping into icy water, tries to turn on the heat in Jasper's van. He gets heat all right... in the form of fire streaming out of the vents, thanks to a squirrel previously biting off the van's heater control valve. This forces both Jasper and Horace to abandon the flaming van and walk by foot.
Horace: (angrily) I can't stand the cold no more.... I WANT HEAT!! (turn on the van's heater on, only for flames to engulf the van's vents) FIRE!!! TOO HOT!!! TOO HOT!!!

tropes.name: Big Damn Heroes
tropes.html: As Lucky was accidentally left when the other puppies escaped from DeVil Manor, and Skinner had just arrived and was about to grab him, Kipper comes to the rescue and fights off Skinner, saving Lucky.

tropes.name: Blue Means Cold
tropes.html: Horace's skin turns blue after he falls into a frozen pond, and he spends a good portion of his screen time afterward shivering.

tropes.name: Bowdlerise
tropes.html: A slight re-dub occurred in the United Kingdom release, in which Horace's line "No bloody wonder you can't talk, mate!" was re-dubbed to "No blinkin' wonder you can't talk, mate!" The "bloody" slang is considered to be profane in the United Kingdom.

tropes.name: Bratty Half-Pint
tropes.html: The kid testing Roger’s Dalmatian starring video games.

tropes.name: Bumbling Henchmen Duo
tropes.html: Jasper and Horace, just like their animated counterparts, are comedic henchmen working for Cruella.

tropes.name: A Cat in a Gang of Dogs
tropes.html: A tabby cat probably based on Sergeant Tibbs from the original animated movie makes a cameo.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
• Anita's drawing of Cruella in a Dalmatian coat. She finds it after Pongo and Perdita run away and realizes that Cruella did take the puppies, to kill them.
  • In the beginning, Anita sees a news report about a rare Siberian tiger in the London Zoo having been killed for her fur, and Horace and Jasper later bring Cruella the tiger's pelt after Skinner finishes preparing it. When the police find the pelt during their raid of Cruella's house, it's more than enough evidence to prove she's taken the puppies and committed more crimes besides.
  • The skunk who takes a nap in Cruella's car as she prepares to retrieve the puppies. She mistakes it for her purse and at the end, it makes its way into the cop car holding Cruella and her henchmen, and sprays all four of them for one last punchline.

tropes.name: Christmas Episode
tropes.html: The scene where the puppies get their collars is suggested to be set during Christmastime, due to its use of Mel Torme's "Christmas Song".

tropes.name: Clever Crows
tropes.html: There is a heroic raven in the barnyard, who calls Pongo and Perlita to report that the lost puppies are there. He then warns the other animals about Cruella's arrival and attacks Cruella before stealing her red hat.

tropes.name: Comically Missing the Point
tropes.html:
There's this exchange after Cruella and her henchmen have been defeated:
Cruella: (addressing Jasper, Horace, and Skinner) Congratulations, you three have won the gold, silver, and bronze medals in the Moron Olympics.
Horace: (after a very long beat) Who won the gold?
Cruella: (screaming) SHUT UP!!

tropes.name: Composite Character
tropes.html: As in the animated film, it combines the book's Missis (Pongo's mate) and Perdita (another female who was brought in as a sort of wet-nurse because there were too many puppies).

tropes.name: Crotch-Glance Sex Check
tropes.html: When Roger mistakes Perdy for Pongo, he lifted her leg to check for her sex.

tropes.name: Darker and Edgier
tropes.html: This film is a good deal grimmer than the original animated version, and even the original book. The opening scenes include a news report about a tiger in a zoo being illegally killed for her skin, showing the lengths Cruella will go to for her furs; Cruella's henchman Mr. Skinner is terrifying; Anita flat-out realizes that Cruella plans to kill the puppies for her coat...

tropes.name: Deadpan Snarker
tropes.html:
• Cruella can be very sarcastic and snarky in the film:
    "Puppies! You have been a busy boy!"
    "(To Jasper after the puppies are stolen) "My faith in your limited intelligence is momentarily restored."
    (To her henchmen in the police van) "Congratulations! You just won gold, silver and bronze in the moron Olympics!"
  • Roger also has his moments:
    (To Pongo about being unable to sell any of his games) "We're fast approaching the point where I'm gonna have to start eating your table scraps."
    "I went swimming in the pond." and Anita taking his sarcasm seriously makes it funnier.

tropes.name: Decomposite Character
tropes.html:
• In the animated film, Horace and Jasper were supposed to kill and skin the puppies themselves. This film introduces the character of Mr. Skinner, who Horace and Jasper are tasked with delivering the puppies to. Though they do consider doing the job themselves when Mr. Skinner is running late.
  • Though Tibbs the cat still makes an appearance, his role as the animal who sneaks the puppies out of the villains' hideout is transferred to a new character, an Airedale Terrier named Kipper.

tropes.name: Demoted to Extra
tropes.html: As noted above, Sgt. Tibbs no longer saves the puppies like in the original, and only makes a brief cameo in the barnyard scene.

tropes.name: Diabolical Dog Catcher
tropes.html: The movie opens with an in-universe case as Roger, who's a video game developer, is working on a game where the player plays as a dog who's running from one of these. The tiredness of the trope is lampshaded as the other devs Roger works with really hate the idea (putting in Cruella to Animals works, though).

tropes.name: Did I Just Say That Out Loud?
tropes.html:
Jasper tries to emphasize to Horace not to comment on Mr. Skinner's huge scar on his throat. First words out of his mouth when Skinner opens the door?
Horace: Oh! Look at the size of that scar! No bloody wonder you can't talk, mate!
Skinner: (Death Glare)
Jasper: Excuse me for a minute. (closes the door and decks Horace)

tropes.name: Disappointed in You
tropes.html: Cruella was displeased when her best employee Anita got married, earlier she tried to discourage her from such things since she believes married/family life would damper her potential, even though it's not for case for Anita. When Anita refuses to sell the puppies to her for any price, Cruella became furious and fires her from her job, proclaiming to her that she'll never work in fashion again.

tropes.name: Dog Walks You
tropes.html: Pongo and later Perdita run after the other, dragging their owners on bikes by the leash. Poor Roger and Anita end up veering out of control and land in the park duck pond.

tropes.name: Dope Slap
tropes.html: Horace gets one from Jasper after loudly pointing out the scar on Skinner's neck when he was specifically told not to.

tropes.name: Double Standard: Abuse, Female on Male
tropes.html: Anita clocking Roger in the head with a handbag full of bricks is played for laughs, albeit she does it to stop him from unwittingly stealing Perdita and is genuinely apologetic when she learns it was a misunderstanding.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Standards
tropes.html:
In spite of serving Cruella, the Badun brothers (particularly Horace) make little to no effort in hiding their discomfort about Skinner's methods of skinning animals for taxidermy.
Jasper (examining one of Skinner's tools): God, bloody gruesome line of work you're in, Skinner.
Horace: The sight of all these deceased creatures gives me a shrinky winky.

tropes.name: Every Scar Has a Story
tropes.html: Jasper tells Horace that Skinner has a horrible scar on his neck from where a dog nearly tore his throat out, rendering him mute, and warns Horace not to ask him about it. Horace immediately forgets this warning upon seeing the scar, and Jasper decks him.

tropes.name: Evil Cannot Comprehend Good
tropes.html:
Cruella cannot understand why Roger and Anita, who are on a fixed income, refuse to sell the puppies, even when she offers them a cheque for £7,500. In fact, her insistence is what convinces them that Cruella's intentions are not in the puppies' favor.
Anita: But Cruella, what would you do with 15 puppies?
Roger: That's irrelevant, Anita. She can't have any of them because they're not for sale!

tropes.name: Evil-Detecting Dog
tropes.html:
• Pongo and Perdita are immediately distrustful of Cruella as they furiously growl and bark at her, knowing that she only wants their puppies for their fur coat. Upon the two dogs' departure, Nanny correctly points out that they just ran off only to look for their puppies. She even points out that dogs themselves have a sixth sense that helps them deduce a person's true nature, just like they did with Cruella. This is what causes Anita, Roger and Nanny to learn that Cruella is responsible for stealing the puppies in the first place; with Anita sadly saying that Cruella wants to kill the puppies only for her spotted fur coat.
  • The local pensioner's pet bulldog furiously barks at Jasper and Horace after they kidnapped the Dalmatian puppies from the Dearly residence, though the pensioner himself doesn't suspect anything. The bulldog's barks were loud enough for Pongo and Perdy to hear, leading them, Roger and Anita to find out what happened. Even Horace lampshades this by pointing out how serious this is, only for Jasper to brush it off.

tropes.name: Evil Laugh
tropes.html: Several impressive examples, courtesy of Cruella.

tropes.name: Evil Is Hammy
tropes.html: Glenn Close knew this was a great role for the application of mountains of ham, and she brought it all with her. Her legendary talent let her pull it off while making it look easy.

tropes.name: Expy
tropes.html:
Mr. Skinner's black coat, hat, and gloves resemble those of Judge Doom.
  • Also noteworthy that in the original book Cruella is married to a taxidermist but Cruella herself is made single, thus Mr Skinner is an Expy for Mr De Vil.

tropes.name: Faint in Shock
tropes.html: Anita goes out cold when she learns she's pregnant.<!--* FauxAffablyEvil: Cruella.-->

tropes.name: Femme Fatalons
tropes.html: One of Cruella's outfits has long, curved fingernails on the outside of her High-Class Gloves.

tropes.name: Flames of Love
tropes.html: Roger and Anita's romance begins with them drying their clothes by the fire. When things get clearly romantic, there's a lingering shot of the clothes catching on fire before a Smash Cut to the characters getting married.

tropes.name: Foe Romantic Subtext
tropes.html: Cruella seems really interested in Anita. She acts like a Woman Scorned upon reading about her marriage announcement in the paper, and says she misses the "interaction" with her at work. It's outright confirmed in the novelization that she had feelings for Anita, and Anita choosing Roger over her is partly what fueled her revenge desire.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html: Very early on in the film Anita happens to catch a news report about a tiger being killed at London Zoo. Younger viewers likely won't realize the meaning of 'excoriated', but then Jasper and Horace pick up an order for Cruella that turns out to be the tiger's pelt.

tropes.name: Four-Temperament Ensemble
tropes.html: Cruella and Jasper are choleric, Horace is phlegmatic / sanguine, and Mr. Skinner is melancholic.

tropes.name: Fourth-Date Marriage
tropes.html: Roger accidentally proposes to Anita on the day they meet, but she accepts.

tropes.name: Freeze-Frame Bonus
tropes.html:
• As often happens, the newspaper articles briefly visible onscreen repeat the same few lines over and over again.
  • When Mr Skinner is totalling the 99 stolen puppies for Cruella, the long list of families that lost their puppies to this dog-napping spree can be seen, with the Dearlys being their latest victims.
    • Wodllars- 10
    • Palmer- 8
    • Wilkinson- 10
    • Wells- 9
    • Ackland- 7
    • Masters- 8
    • Calleja- 6
    • Graham- 7
    • Tomkins- 12
    • Gorton- 7
    • Dearly- 15

tropes.name: Friend-or-Idol Decision
tropes.html: Cruella, Anita's boss, offers to take the puppies, to buy them. While Roger declares they're not for sale, Anita is a bit hesitant at first because of the money being offered, and because refusing your boss is not necessarily a good idea. Then Cruella shouts at them to take it, and Anita finally puts her foot down by quietly refusing the offer. She's not surprised when Cruella fires her and threatens to blacklist her from working in the fashion industry again.

tropes.name: Graceful Loser
tropes.html: After failing to catch the dogs one too many times, Jasper and Horace willingly turn themselves in upon seeing the police cars.

tropes.name: Gross-Out Show
tropes.html: A pig farts in Cruella's face, she falls into a vat of molasses, is kicked by a horse into a pigsty, and sprayed by a skunk that she mistakes for her handbag. There's also Wizzer, the puppy who is constantly peeing.

tropes.name: Handbag of Hurt
tropes.html: At the start of the movie, Anita uses her purse to attack Roger, believing he was intentionally trying to take Perdy. This purse also contains three bricks, which delivered a solid blow to Roger’s unsuspecting face.

tropes.name: Heroic Dog
tropes.html:
• Kipper the Airedale Terrier launches a rescue mission to save the 99 stolen puppies from Cruella and her minions. When he realizes that he missed one, he goes back to the mansion and rescues Lucky from Skinner before the man can lay a hand on the scared puppy.
  • Colonel is also part of the rescue mission the puppies by leading them to the farm where they’re safe and well-fed until Pongo and Perdy arrive. He also manages to hide them under a flock of sheep, thereby avoiding Cruella when she drives by the field.

tropes.name: Hollywood Game Design
tropes.html: Roger's profession is updated from music composer to games designer. The process of making a game apparently involves him taking a game (which he presumably made on his own) to a group of suits who let an obnoxious child review it (apparently having played it for a few minutes) and give him feedback.

tropes.name: "Home Alone" Antics
tropes.html: Jasper and Horace suffer all kinds of humiliations (Jasper nearly gets impaled by a mounted moose's antlers, Horace falls into a freezing pond, etc.). Of course, this movie was written and produced by John Hughes.

tropes.name: Harmless Freezing
tropes.html: Horace, though he's still blue and shivering in the next scene.

tropes.name: Hoist by Her Own Petard
tropes.html: Cruella's love of fur includes having a rare Siberian tiger illegally slaughtered for her pelt; later, she organizes the theft of Pongo and Perdy's litter to spite their owners. On top of the dogs finding and rescuing all the puppies she was planning to use for her coat, Anita and Roger were already suspicious of Cruella after her fury at being denied the puppies, so they realize what she's planning and get the Metropolitan Police to raid her house, where the discovery of the tiger pelt alone is enough to get a warrant for her arrest.

tropes.name: Human-Focused Adaptation
tropes.html: Sort of. Because none of the animals talk in this version, the humans get more focus and screen time.

tropes.name: Humiliation Conga
tropes.html: The villains end up getting this. Horace and Jasper are reduced to staggering through the woods after suffering a Groin Attack via electric fence, to the point where they find being arrested a relief. Cruella, after constantly being tricked and stalled by the farm animals, ends up covered in molasses, mud and pig manure. And when they finally all end up in a police van — along with Mr. Skinner, who's come out worse for wear from being mauled by a dog — it turns out there's also a skunk in there with them, who starts spraying. Cue the screaming.

tropes.name: Ignore the Disability
tropes.html:
Jasper and Horace are meeting with the skinner who has a large animal attack scar on his neck and can't speak. Jasper tries to emphasize to Horace not to comment about Mr. Skinner's huge scar on his throat. First words out of his mouth when Skinner opens the door?
Horace: Ah! Look at the size of that scar! No bloody wonder you can't talk, mate!
Skinner: (death glare)
Jasper: 'Scuse me just a minute, would you? (closes the door and decks Horace)

tropes.name: Iron Butt-Monkey
tropes.html:
• Horace. He slips on the ice, winds up crashing through a window, slides across the battlements, and drops 20 feet into icy water. None of this kills him.
  • Cruella gets kicked across a farmyard by a horse, has a massive pig land on her,, covered in hay, thrown into a vat of molasses, and is catapulted through a high window and down into a pig sty. None of this kills or even hurts her.

tropes.name: Know When to Fold Them
tropes.html:
• Jasper and Horace are only too happy to surrender to the police after getting the crap beaten out of them.
  • Downplayed with Cruella. After being subjected to so much humiliation by the animals (covered in hay and molasses and thrown into a pigpen), Cruella finds herself caught by the police, who declares that they found her tiger-skinned coat (thanks to a complaint filed by Anita and Roger), her plot to skin the puppies have been exposed and she will be facing charges for her crimes. However, rather than spewing out a tantrum as usual, Cruella instead swallows her pride and accepts her fate, though she takes out her frustration against her henchmen (who are also arrested) inside the police van.
    Cruella: (realizing that she's about to be arrested after her plan is exposed) Oh.... (curls up her dirty streak of hair from her face) ....is there something wrong?

tropes.name: Live-Action Cartoon
tropes.html: Among a lot of things like Cartoon Physics, Cruella’s over-the-top wardrobe and personality, the animals high-fiving and the villains getting pummeled in cartoonish ways.

tropes.name: Lost in Imitation
tropes.html: Naturally seems to be based more on the 1961 film than on the book. Though unlike the first film, it does get Roger and Anita's last names from the original book right: Dearly instead of Radcliffe. Also, the sequel includes the dinner party from the book, which was not included in the original film.

tropes.name: Love at First Sight
tropes.html: Pongo is instantly enamored when he first sees Perdita going by him, with her giving him a friendly bark.

tropes.name: Mass "Oh, Crap!"
tropes.html:
• Cruella and her minions, when they realize her handbag is a pissed off skunk that they're locked in a confined space with.
  • The puppies, upon being terrified by Cruella's design in Roger's video game.

tropes.name: Meaningful Name
tropes.html:
• The named puppies all have these: Lucky has a horseshoe-shaped patch around his eye (he's "lucky" to be alive after almost dying at birth and he's extremely lucky that Kipper went back to look for any stragglers), Jewel has a series of spots around her neck that resemble a necklace, Dipstick has a tail that's half black and half white, Fidget is constantly itchy, Two-Tone has all her spots concentrated on one side of her body, and Wizzer has poor bladder control.
  • Mr. Skinner skins animals.

tropes.name: Minecart Madness
tropes.html: In a Setting Update, Roger is a video game designer rather than a songwriter — part of the film's Dénouement shows that his skills have improved by showing off the final level of his game, which is a 3D minecart escape sequence playtested by a boy. It begins with two puppies driving on rails across a dark mine full of hazards, needing to lean whenever they approach a curve or hazard; a TNT barrel bounces across the rails, and Cruella attempts to reach the puppies only to get hit by the barrel, making it explode. It's so thrilling that even the dogs seeing the boy play the game show unanimous emotions of concern or excitement. The boy is also impressed by the game.

tropes.name: Misplaced Wildlife
tropes.html: Raccoons and a skunk in England. Justified in a bizarre way. There are feral populations of raccoons and skunks in England. Long story short, they were bred for the fur trade (and as exotic pets) but ended up escaping into the wild and breeding. It's not so much a case of misplaced wildlife in fiction, but rather a case of misplaced wildlife in Real Life.

tropes.name: Mythology Gag
tropes.html:
• The Dalmatian that appears in Roger's video game strong resembles Pongo's animated counterpart. The puppies at the end (Patches and Wizzer) similarly look like they’re lifted from the animated film.
  • Also, Cruella. In the game, she chases after the puppies in her car like in the animated film and sports her animated counterpart's Nightmare Face.
  • When the puppies are about to receive their collars, they are shown watching TV much like in the original film when they watched Thunderbolt. Here they are shown watching Disney's own The Aristocats, during the closing of the "Everybody Wants to be a Cat" sequence, and Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey, showing Shadow being reunited with Peter.
  • When Roger tries (but fails) to design a convincing villain for his video game with Pongo by his side shortly after his wedding to Anita, the devilish dog catcher he attempts to design bears a striking resemblance to the villain Dirty Dawson in The Thuderbolt Adventure Hour, the show that the Dalmatian family were watching in the original movie.

tropes.name: Never My Fault
tropes.html: In the end, Cruelly furiously blames Jasper, Horace and Skinner for her arrest by calling them incompetent twits; she had failed to realize that Anita and Roger filed a complaint against her, which led the police to discover Cruella's tiger-skinned coat in her mansion, thus deducing her plot to kidnap and skin the puppies.

tropes.name: Nice Job Breaking It, Hero!
tropes.html: In this version, Cruella gets the idea for a Dalmatian skin coat from a sketch that Anita draws inspired by Perdita's fur. Though of course, Anita never meant for the coat to be made of real fur.

tropes.name: Nice Job Fixing It, Villain!
tropes.html: Cruella stealing Pongo and Perdy's litter to spite Anita and Roger ends up causing her downfall. The dogs muster the Twilight Bark, go to rescue their children and ruin her operation in Suffolk; meanwhile, the humans naturally suspect Cruella of organizing the theft, Anita thinks back to the Dalmatian skin coat she designed, she puts two and two together and they immediately call the police to search the de Vil house.

tropes.name: Nightmare Retardant
tropes.html: In-universe, Roger's attempt at making an interesting villain for his video game, which is a devilish dog catcher. Pongo just yawns.

tropes.name: Not His Sled
tropes.html: Although much of this film follows the same story beats as the animated version, the climax is completely different. In the animated version, the Dalmatians escape in a moving van, a car chase ensues, and the villains are defeated when they crash their own vehicles. In the live-action version, there is no moving van and no car chase. Instead, the story resolves with the police showing up to arrest the villains and take the Dalmatians back to London.

tropes.name: Of Corsets Sexy
tropes.html: Cruella wears a cheetah striped one when she tries to buy the puppies.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html: After Pongo and Perdita run to find the puppies, Anita and Roger are talking with Nanny and considering the possibility of Cruella taking the puppies for revenge. Upon Nanny explaining that dogs have a sixth sense that can help them deduce a person's true intents, Anita remembers her Dalmatian coat drawing that Cruella was so ecstatic over and shows it to Roger and Nanny, announcing with horror that Cruella is going to kill the puppies to make the coat. Cue Mass "Oh, Crap!" from all of them.

tropes.name: Ooh, Me Accent's Slipping
tropes.html: Glenn Close. Her American accent is constantly poking through in the vowels. And right before that when Anita tells Cruella that she's having a baby, "You know what they say, accidents may happen!"

tropes.name: Panicky Expectant Father
tropes.html: Roger is nervous enough during the birth of Pongo's puppies and wonders how he's going to react when his own baby arrives.

tropes.name: Pedal-to-the-Metal Shot
tropes.html: There is a shot of Jasper stepping on the gas when he is trying to revive the car, blowing the smoke in Horace's face.

tropes.name: Pet the Dog
tropes.html: Cruella does genuinely appreciate Anita's hard work and talent, praising her for her designs and remarking that any fashion house would be lucky to have her. When Anita mentions that she hopes to marry someday, Cruella sincerely warns her not to throw away her career for a man's sake. There's even a small moment when Cruella examines Anita's spotted dress and asks her permission to add a cape instead of altering the design on her own. All told, Cruella seems to value her relationship with Anita.<!--* PimpedOutDress: Some of Cruella's outfits.-->

tropes.name: Product Placement
tropes.html: A noticeable Dr. Pepper can is seen in the first scene with Herbert testing the game.

tropes.name: Punny Name
tropes.html: The puppy who constantly pees is named Wizzer.

tropes.name: Put on a Prison Bus
tropes.html: Towards the end of the film, Horace and Jasper willingly surrender to the police and find Skinner upon entering the van. Later, Cruella joins the trio thanks to the police having an arrest warrant for her after finding the tiger-skinner coat in her mansion. While Cruella is put on probation in the sequel (only to get arrested again in the end after she relapses on her dog hunt), Horace and Jasper are absent due to having remained arrested ever since.

tropes.name: Rascally Raccoon
tropes.html: Aside from the dogs rescuing the puppies, they also receive a lot of help from raccoons who help stall Horace, Jasper and Cruella. They sabotage Horace and Jasper’s truck and manage to distract them by playing in their truck, giving Kipper enough time to get the puppies out. They also drop Cruella in a vat of molasses when she’s trying to get her hat back from a raccoon.

tropes.name: "The Reason You Suck" Speech
tropes.html:
After Cruella De Vil and her henchmen have been defeated and are being carted off to prison by the police, she has this to say:
Cruella: My business, my reputation, my life, has been ruined because you three incompetent twits let yourselves be outsmarted by a bunch of dumb animals! And you call yourselves men? HA! I've seen more intelligent pieces of carpet!

tropes.name: Rollercoaster Mine
tropes.html: In the ending, Roger designs a video game about dalmatian puppies riding a mine cart and fighting Cruella as the final boss.

tropes.name: Setting Update
tropes.html: Among other things, Roger is a video game designer.

tropes.name: Slapstick
tropes.html: Roger falls into a lake after Pongo drags him on his bike. A few minutes later Perdy does the same thing to Anita. Also, out of all the villains, Cruella gets the most physical comedy by the end and is covered head to toe in mud.

tropes.name: Smelly Skunk
tropes.html: Cruella De Vil mistook a sleeping skunk for her black mink stole. When she and her fellow dog-nappers got arrested and put in the back of the paddy-wagon, the skunk wakes up, and EVERYONE gets sprayed!

tropes.name: Stocking Mask
tropes.html: Horace and Jasper wear stockings over their heads before forcing their way into Anita and Roger's home to lock the nanny in a cupboard before kidnapping the puppies. Played for Laughs in a previous scene when they both get their heads in the same stocking and struggle to get out of the van.

tropes.name: Suddenly Shouting
tropes.html:
Cruella. Which prompted Anita herself to tell her off.
Cruella: (offers the check) Take it. (the Dearlys are hesitant, then cue Dramatic Thunder) TAKE IT!!!!

tropes.name: Suddenly Voiced
tropes.html: Skinner, but only at the end of the film when the skunk starts spraying, when he does make one shriek of horror while banging on the van like a traumatized child.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Realistic Outcome
tropes.html:
• When the puppies are born, Cruella tries to take them immediately when learning their spots come later. Anita refuses to allow this by pointing out that the puppies have to be with their mother for several weeks. Besides which, they're not selling the puppies just like that.
  • Unlike the animated film, where she dismissed Roger's accusation of Cruella, Anita herself pieces together that Cruella was behind the puppies' kidnapping. Police Are Useless is also not in effect here, as the law immediately get a warrant to raid Cruella's house when she becomes a suspect, finding the tiger fur — already the subject of a criminal investigation — to prove that Cruella is guilty. Cruella is then arrested as soon as they find her in the countryside.

tropes.name: Surrounded by Idiots
tropes.html:
After all three villains are arrested, Cruella reflects on their failure and begins to chastise her henchmen for their incompetence:
Cruella: Congratulations. You three have just won the Gold, Silver, and Bronze in the Morons Olympics!
Horace: Who won the gold?
Cruella: SHUT UP!

tropes.name: Sycophantic Servant
tropes.html:
Cruella's assistant, Frederick. He even admits to it:
Cruella: What kind of a sycophant are you?
Frederick: Ummm.... what kind of a sycophant would you like me to be?

tropes.name: Tagline
tropes.html: "So many dogs, so little time"

tropes.name: Take That!
tropes.html: In-universe. At the end of the film, Roger adds Cruella to his video game as the villain.

tropes.name: Tempting Fate
tropes.html: An unhinged Cruella rants about being victorious yet against the Dalmatians and all the other farm animals and then yells that she will have the last laugh, laughing maniacally as she does so. The farm animals, in a kind of example of a Shut Up, Hannibal!, kick her out of the barn and into a pigpen. Moments later, the police shows up to arrest her. Clearly, that was her last laugh.

tropes.name: This Is My Human
tropes.html: Pongo, at least, considers himself the Master of the household.

tropes.name: Title Drop
tropes.html: "I've counted 98 puppies. The two adults make it 100 even. [...]Make that 101 Dalmatians, sir."

tropes.name: Truer to the Text
tropes.html: A minor case but the couple being named "Dearly" instead of "Radcliffe" makes it somewhat more faithful despite being Lost in Imitation.

tropes.name: Urine Trouble
tropes.html: Whizzer pees on a magazine cover with Cruella de Vil's face on it during the escape. This is also his entire shtick.

tropes.name: Vanity License Plate
tropes.html: Cruella's license plate reads DEV IL.

tropes.name: Vile Villain, Saccharine Show
tropes.html: Zigzagged for Mr. Skinner. While Cruella is this as well, she is hammy and laughably evil at times. But with Skinner, there are no such moments, apart from Horace's comments. He never utters any dialogue because a dog tore open his throat (with a visible scar shown), and he has a permanent leer on his face. His job is basically skinning animals and turning them into coats for Cruella. He was about to do so to Lucky, until Kipper mauls Skinner with a shot in the shadows. He is terrifying as a result. Notably, he does not encounter any slapstick in the film like Horace, Jasper, or even Cruella. However, he comically panicked and banged inside the police van like a scared child when the skunk started spraying against him and the other villains.

tropes.name: Villainous Exit Denied
tropes.html:
After the Humiliation Conga that Jasper and Horace suffer, they promptly stagger through the woods, defeated. When the two happen to run across the police moments later, they willingly surrender. (After all the crap they've been through, they're actually happy to turn themselves in.)
Jasper: Thank the Lord.
Horace: We're saved!

tropes.name: Wacky Marriage Proposal
tropes.html: Roger proposes to Anita via a Freudian Slip: "Would you like another cup of marriage? I mean tea?"

tropes.name: Wide Eyes and Shrunken Irises
tropes.html: This happens to the animated Cruella DeVil in the video game Roger made when a keg of dynamite is thrown at her.

tropes.name: Worst News Judgment Ever
tropes.html:
• Why do National Newspapers like The Independent have reports on two relative nobodies getting married? Or make the kidnapping of fifteen puppies front page headline news? While Anita did work as a fashion designer for Cruella's fashion house and she and Cruella are on a First-Name Basis, there's little on-screen to imply she's particularly notable within the company - Cruella's only really interested in Anita's work when she designs the coat (her original idea being for FAKE fur). On the other hand, Cruella does try to discourage Anita from getting married out of fear of squandering her talent, so it might be that Anita is more up-and-coming than we really see in story. Based on the other articles, the wedding was probably announced in the 'Births, Deaths and Marriage' section. Most English newspapers have them, some even include pictures.
  • The final headline about Cruella getting arrested makes more sense, since she's the owner of a famous fashion house and they've already linked her to the illegal killing of an endangered Siberian tiger and the attempted skinning of helpless Dalmatian puppies.

tropes.name: Comic Trio
tropes.html: Phil leads, Stu complains, and Alan (the one that caused the mayhem in the first place) goes along with it.

tropes.name: Denser and Wackier
tropes.html: The sequels become more absurd and slapsticky than the first film, while reoccurring character Chow gets flanderized in his subsequent appearances.

tropes.name: Distressed Dude
tropes.html:
• Subverted with Doug and Teddy in the first two films — the only danger they're in comes from it taking two days to find them in the isolated locations they're trapped in and not of any direct threats on their lives.
  • Played straight in the third film, as Doug is kidnapped and held hostage as incentive for the Wolfpack to track Chow down after he stole millions from Marshall.

tropes.name: DIY Dentistry
tropes.html: Stu is missing a tooth when they wake up from the night they can't remember. At the end, it's revealed that he pulled it out himself because the others said he couldn't do it. For extra irony points, Stu himself is a dentist, for all the difference it makes when yanking out a tooth with pliers at a strip club while black-out drunk.

tropes.name: Four-Man Band
tropes.html:
• Only Sane Man: Doug, the most levelheaded of the Wolfpack.
  • The Smart Guy: Phil, who figures out most of the places where the Wolfpack was the night before.
  • The Pervert: Alan, the stupid Manchild who started all this shit.
  • Butt-Monkey: Stu, who has the worst things happen to him.

tropes.name: Four-Philosophy Ensemble
tropes.html:
• Stu: The Cynic, always finding something to complain about.
  • Doug: The Optimist, the mild-mannered bridegroom who is nice to everyone.
  • Phil: The Realist, who takes charge of the search for Doug.
  • Alan: The Apathetic, always has his head in the clouds and caused all this shit to go down in the first place.

tropes.name: Four-Temperament Ensemble
tropes.html: Alan is Sanguine, Phil is Choleric, Stu is Melancholic and Doug is Phlegmatic.

tropes.name: Freudian Trio
tropes.html: Alan (id), Phil (ego) and Stu (superego).

tropes.name: Genre Throwback
tropes.html: A mundane, vulgar and gritty one to the Screwball Comedy genre of the 1930s and 40s for it's premise and the tropes the trilogy upholds. The main three of the Wolf Pack is a down-to-earth Expy of The Three Stooges, while Doug himself can be considered an Expy of Ted Healy, whom the Stooges were lackeys of in the early days. The first film's scene has a Shout-Out to Howard Hawks' Bringing Up Baby, while the racial stereotype character of Leslie Chow would not look out of place from a film from the 30s and 40s where the racial imperium was the norminvoked. Alan himself mostly thinks he's in one of the era's films when they abide by The Hays Code back then if his tendency to Gosh Dang It to Heck! is taken to consideration. Todd's real life experience that inspired the making of the first film can be considered the closest to a screwball comedy film-like situation in real-life.

tropes.name: Good Cannot Comprehend Evil
tropes.html: When Stu tries to give Melissa a dressing-down, all he can come up is "you're... a bad person!".

tropes.name: Gosh Dang It to Heck!
tropes.html:
Alan. So much. While pretty much every character in the series is not afraid of dropping a few f-bombs, Alan absolutely refuses. There are examples from all three films, but this exchange from the first movie sums it up quite nicely.
Phil: GOD DAMN IT!
Alan: Gosh darn it!
Phil: SHIT!
Alan: Shoot!

tropes.name: How We Got Here
tropes.html: Part of each film shows the Wolfpack in various situations, and then they slowly retrace their steps. The third film subverts it, because they didn't get wasted like in the first two films until the very end of the film at least, but events that happened in the first film end up becoming important points in the third one.

tropes.name: Insistent Terminology
tropes.html:
• Stu repeatedly calling himself a doctor in the first film, only for both Phil and the doctor who examined Phil to correct him by pointing out he's "really only a dentist."
  • Inverted in Part II, after Phil gets shot in the arm — Phil asks Stu to check his wound because he's a doctor, and Stu insists he's just a dentist to try & get out of it.
  • Subverted in Part III when Phil attempts to motivate Stu by telling him "You. Are. A. Doctor". It works.

tropes.name: Interchangeable Asian Cultures
tropes.html: Chinese Mr. Chow is played by Korean Ken Jeong, and Thai siblings Teddy and Lauren are Chinese and Korean respectively (and don't look remotely Thai).

tropes.name: Large Ham
tropes.html: Alan, along with Stu and Leslie Chow.

tropes.name: Living Prop
tropes.html: Stephanie, Phil's wife, has one line in each film and is never named on screen. This applies even more so in Part II where she spends her brief screentime hovering silently at Phil's shoulder, and her one line comes amidst several characters speaking at the same time when Alan runs a speedboat aground and everyone is checking to make sure the guys are okay.

tropes.name: Mundane MacGuffin Person
tropes.html: Doug, who is given all the characterization of a very Nice Guy to both his friends and brother in law. So much so that you can honestly believe these guys would shake down all of Las Vegas to find him.

tropes.name: Made of Iron
tropes.html:
All of the Wolfpack appear to be this.
  • In the first film Alan takes a stun gun to the face, a crowbar to the face, and a Mike Tyson punch to the face, all within one day. Phil is tased in the crotch, attacked by Chow with a crowbar, clawed by a tiger and on the side of the car that gets T-Boned. Finally, Stu is tased in the neck, hit in the crotch with a crowbar and rips out his own tooth.
  • In Part II all three guys are repeatedly beaten with a long stick of bamboo by a monk, and Phil gets shot in the friggin' arm but manages to get by fine with a few $6 stitches. Made of iron, indeed.

tropes.name: Noodle Incident
tropes.html:
• Oh so subverted. At first it looks like the events of last night couldn't ever be anything but this, but by the end of the movie, the characters have a pretty good idea of what they did, and it lives up. Played straight, as they never get to know where they found the chicken (a popular theory is that they tried to feed it to the tiger) or how the chair ended up on fire.
  • It's never been explained why Alan can't be within 200 feet of an elementary school or a Chuck E. Cheese, though this could be because he picks fights with children (see Manchild above). Zach Galifinakis says in the DVD commentary that Alan innocently tried to play with some children which of course looked suspicious to parents. It was all just a misunderstanding.
  • "What are you talking about? I've found a baby before."
  • In the second film, the guys somehow managed to start a riot, which brought out the police and left part of Bangkok in ruins.
  • Played straight in the The Stinger of the third movie. The Wolfpack have another wild night they can’t remember, but unlike the previous movies, it's never revealed what happened.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html: The first two movies are full of these moments, particularly right after the guys wake up.

tropes.name: Only Sane Man
tropes.html: Doug, and to a lesser extent, Phil. Stu would qualify if not for his tendency to completely flip out over (sometimes) minor things.

tropes.name: Photo Montage
tropes.html: Happens during the credits of the first two films to show what happened during their respective nights.

tropes.name: Post–Wake-Up Realization
tropes.html: Alan wakes up after they were all hungover and not noticing that there's a tiger in the bathroom.

tropes.name: Serial Escalation
tropes.html: Every time it looks like they've got a handle on what they did, something even worse makes itself known.

tropes.name: Signature Style
tropes.html: The Dan Band.

tropes.name: The Smurfette Principle
tropes.html: All three lead characters are male and most secondary characters with substantial screentime such as Doug, Mr. Chow and Teddy are male too. The first film has more of a female presence since Jade (Heather Graham's character) gets a fairly big supporting role but her counterpart in Part II appears in only one scene and the only other female characters with more than a couple of lines are Tracy and Lauren.

tropes.name: Team Power Walk
tropes.html:
Happens in all three films, all of which are soundtracked to a Kanye West song.
  • In the first movie, when they are hitting the casino to the tune of "Can't Tell Me Nothing."
  • In the second movie, when they are leaving the airport to the tune of "Stronger."
  • In the third third movie, walking out to Alan's wedding to the tune of "Dark Fantasy."

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html: In the sequels, Chow's two henchmen have not been seen since the first movie.

tropes.name: World of Jerkass
tropes.html: With the exception of Stu, Doug, Jade, and Lauren, pretty much everyone is either an apathetic jerk, a criminal, or downright insane.

tropes.name: Accidental Marriage
tropes.html: Because you can't have a party in Las Vegas without somebody taking a spontaneous trip down the aisle.

tropes.name: Air Drums
tropes.html:
Mike Tyson, when the guys are in his hotel room.
Mike: Shh, shh... This is my favorite part coming up right now.

tropes.name: Alcohol-Induced Idiocy
tropes.html: Obviously. Except it's not from alcohol, it's from being unknowingly drugged.

tropes.name: Animeland
tropes.html:
When a naked, angry Asian man jumps out of the trunk of the car, Alan instantly tries to calm him down by saying that he hates Godzilla too.
  • If you pay attention to Chow's face, it can become a funny moment: he leaves because he's just so confused by the Godzilla line.

tropes.name: Anywhere but Their Lips
tropes.html: Among the first clues that Stu's girl really isn't right for him is that she won't let him kiss her on the lips.

tropes.name: Apathetic Teacher
tropes.html: Phil pretty much doesn't give a rat's ass about the kids in his class.

tropes.name: Armor-Piercing Question
tropes.html: When Stu is confronted by Melissa, she angrily asks him why he went to Las Vegas. This causes Melissa to breakdown and shout at him, causing them to break up.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Law
tropes.html: Needing a large amount of money to get Doug back, the trio go to a blackjack table where Alan wins over $80,000 by counting cards, despite the other guys telling him earlier it's illegal. The thing is, Alan's method of counting cards was not illegal. He didn't use any outside devices or receive instructions from a partner, so he didn't break any laws.

tropes.name: Asian Rudeness
tropes.html: Leslie Chow qualifies, with his aggressiveness and insults.

tropes.name: Beast in the Building
tropes.html: The main characters wake up after a blackout drunk bachelor party to a trashed hotel suite full of unexplained items, including a live chicken. When Alan goes to the bathroom, it takes him a moment to realize there's a tiger with him. They stole it from Mike Tyson.

tropes.name: The Cameo
tropes.html: Mike Tyson as himself. Also Carrot Top and Wayne Newton during the end credits photo montage.

tropes.name: Catchphrase
tropes.html:
Phil says "No shit it's X" often enough during the course of the movie for it to count as one.
  • Phil also says "No, this is good!" every time they remember something terrible from the night before. Stu eventually calls him on it.
  • Alan: "That's classic!"
  • Stu: "WHAT THE FUCK IS GOING ON?!"

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
• Or his ring, in this case. As soon as the Holocaust ring is introduced, you know something is going to happen to it. Stu uses it when he gets married to a hooker.
  • Also, the "This Door Locks Behind You" sign on the door to the roof was a pretty obvious sign that somebody was getting locked up there at some point — though by the time they found Doug, it had long been forgotten.. Possibly a Brick Joke.
  • The tiger. Mike Tyson's tiger.
  • Alan's card counting book, which leads to the Chekhov's Skill.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gunman
tropes.html: As the guys are waking up, a woman is leaving the room. It turns that she actually married Stu the night before.<!--* ChekhovsSkill: Card-counting.-->

tropes.name: Comically Missing the Point
tropes.html: Stu is more concerned that his friends get it right who his girlfriend cheated on him with (a bartender, not a bellhop) than with the fact that she cheated on him in the first place.

tropes.name: Cool Car
tropes.html: You'll never see a finer example of a 1969 Mercedes-Benz convertible on film. Too bad they gradually smash the shit out of it as the movie goes on.

tropes.name: Creator Cameo
